entries.title: California Democrat Rep. Gomez resigns following ethics report on sexual misconduct allegations
entries.summary: California Congressman Rep. Jimmy Gomez says he will resign after a House Ethics report concluded Gomez's actions violated House rules by "making unwelcome sexual advances."
entries.content:
Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., says he is resigning from Congress after a bipartisan investigation released Monday found "substantial evidence" he engaged in sexual misconduct toward a House staffer.

The House Ethics Committee concluded Gomez violated House rules by "making unwelcome sexual advances and engaging in unwelcome sexual conduct towards a House staffer and disregarding the power imbalance inherent in his relationship with House staffers."

The report also says the behavior could constitute criminal sexual assault.

Gomez has served in Congress since 2017 representing parts of Los Angeles. He lost reelection this fall to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres. California uses a system where the top two vote-getters no matter the party advance to the general election. Gomez says his resignation will be effective Dec. 1.

Lisa Banks and Sarah Nesbitt, attorneys for the unnamed House staffer, wrote in a statement that their client testified to the committee truthfully and at personal risk.

"She sacrificed her own sense of safety and privacy to help reveal the ongoing misogyny and debauchery that permeates Capitol Hill," Banks and Nesbitt wrote. "Representative Gomez seems to believe that the power he wields, both as a man and as a member of Congress, makes him untouchable. Today's findings are a meaningful step toward dismantling that belief."

In a statement announcing his plan to resign, Gomez wrote that he cooperated with the investigation, but has strong disagreements with the report and its conclusions.

"Among other significant deficiencies and omissions, the report does not include key portions of my testimony that are essential to a full and fair understanding of what occurred," he wrote.

"I also have serious concerns about the process. In my interview, I answered the Committee's questions only to see my statements selectively quoted, disparaged, and disregarded throughout the final report, to which I was given no opportunity to respond."

The House Ethics Committee, which includes five Democrats and five Republicans, opened its investigation into Gomez in August following a press report of Gomez kissing a staffer from another Congressional office at a party. Gomez denied those allegations.

The committee asked Gomez to disclose whether he "ever engaged in a romantic or sexual relationship or made sexual contact with a congressional staffer." Gomez disclosed interactions with two women — telling the committee the encounters were all consensual. Both women spoke to the committee.

One denied "she had ever had a nonconsensual sexual encounter" with Gomez. The other, described as Witness 1 in the report, said she had more than one encounter with Gomez and she did not consider them consensual.

She told investigators that Gomez made sexual contact without her consent at a bar in February 2024 and then was forceful with her and tried to kiss her at his congressional office in July 2024.

Gomez denied the interactions were nonconsensual. The staffer, described as Witness 1 in the committee report, eventually left her job on Capitol Hill.

"Here, the House lost Witness 1 as a competent and able staffer because of Representative Gomez's misconduct and because of a broader culture of disrespect and toxic sexual behavior toward staff that permeates life on the Hill and is long overdue for correction," the committee wrote.

The report comes amid a broader conversation about how Congress deals with the behavior of its members, especially when it comes to sexual misconduct.

In April, Democrat Eric Swalwell of California resigned his House seat amid allegations of sexual assault and misconduct. He also denied the allegations. Rep. Tony Gonzales (R-Tex.) also resigned from the House after admitting to an affair with a former staff member.

Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) dropped his reelection bid earlier this year after the House Ethics Committee recommended he face a censure vote for allegedly harassing two young female staffers. Edwards denied the allegations.

Republican Reps. Max Miller of Ohio and Cory Mills of Florida also face House Ethics investigations stemming from allegations of domestic violence. Both deny wrongdoing.

Miller lost his reelection bid this fall and Mills lost his GOP primary.

Last week, the House Ethics Committee adopted new rules with the aim of speeding up investigations into sexual misconduct and improving transparency.

entries.title: They attended Trump's controversial meme coin dinner. It didn't go well
entries.summary: Trump held another meme coin dinner for top holders of his cryptocurrency — an event that has raised intense controversy. Here's an inside account from two guests who attended.
entries.content:
They attended Trump’s controversial meme coin dinner. It didn’t go well

Trump held another meme coin dinner for top holders of his cryptocurrency — an event that has raised intense controversy. Here's an inside account from two guests who attended.

JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:

With Democrats winning majorities in Congress, President Trump will likely face investigations into the billions of dollars he and his family have made in crypto. Despite that, the president held another dinner last night to reward the top holders of his meme coin, a cryptocurrency he launched right before his inauguration. NPR's Rafael Nam talked with two people who were there.

RAFAEL NAM, BYLINE: Crypto investor Morten Christensen was among the over a hundred guests who gathered at Trump's golf club on a damp evening in Northern Virginia. He was there to attend what was promoted as the most exclusive dinner in the world. He brought along his little sister. They rode together in an Uber.

MORTEN CHRISTENSEN: Yeah. I'm excited. It's always nice to dress up for an event. My sister looks amazing.

NAM: Christensen has attended these events before. This time, it was a lot less expensive. The coin has cratered in price. By using a sophisticated trading strategy, he says they were basically going for free. His sister, Gabrielle Felen, was decked out in a nice black dress.

GABRIELLE FELEN: Yeah. I'm also excited, a little bit nervous, but excited about how it's going to be.

NAM: Christensen and Felen have agreed to share voice memos through the night, and the three of us buckled in for the event. Trump's crypto events are controversial. The top holders of the coin get to spend time with the president. The more you buy, the closer the access. In the past, many of the attendees have not been from the U.S., raising concerns that Trump could be influenced, which the White House denies. Inside the swanky gala room, Christensen rattles off the people he's met.

CHRISTENSEN: One was from Saudi. One was from London. Met a couple of people from Ukraine, two people from India, four from China. I think one was from South Korea.

NAM: Christensen and Felen are also from abroad, from the Netherlands. They say it's not Trump's politics that drew them to the event. Christensen even believes meme coins are stupid, but it was a chance to see the leader of the free world up close and mingle with guests like Kevin O'Leary from "Shark Tank." But just as they got there, things started taking a turn. He thought he was on the VIP list.

CHRISTENSEN: I got into the entrance, and they said, I'm not on the VIP list, even though I have the email of VIP and everything, and they just said, I'm not on the list, so...

NAM: And just as they started getting ready for the president to walk in, a couple of people approached Christensen. He was getting kicked out for posting pictures online and talking to people in the media, like me. He ended up all the way outside the golf club in the middle of soaking rain.

CHRISTENSEN: So I got removed from the event, from the Trump gala. I'm not sure why.

NAM: NPR did not get a response from organizers as to why. At the golf course, they both decided Felen would stay. She had come all this way to see the president, and she finally got the moment she was waiting for.

UNIDENTIFIED MUSICAL ARTIST: (Singing) God bless the USA.

(CHEERING)

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: Long live Donald Trump.

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Do you want to hear another one (ph)? Should we keep the song going?

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: Yeah.

NAM: Trump went on to deliver a speech that veered everywhere, from crypto to digs on Biden - a speech that Christensen never got to hear.

CHRISTENSEN: It happens, you know. It's a different kind of experience this time around - could have been better for me. But I will just laugh about it.

NAM: Felen enjoyed hearing Trump, but she also felt for her brother.

FELEN: I was definitely disappointed for him, especially when, later, I saw that some people who were in VIP actually got, like, a one-on-one selfie with Trump, so probably also got to shake his hand, say some words. So that would have been a great opportunity.

NAM: As they departed the U.S., Christensen and Felen weren't as excited anymore. Like many who have purchased the Trump meme coin, they had a different feeling - disappointment.

Rafael Nam, NPR News.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

entries.title: Some women in tech have concerns about Huang's return
entries.summary: Women who have advocated for DEI in tech say Jensen Huang's return to NVIDIA as CEO sends a message that in Silicon Valley, all that matters is money. s
entries.content:
Women who have advocated for DEI in tech say Jensen Huang's return to NVIDIA as CEO sends a message that in Silicon Valley, all that matters is money. s

JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:

Late this morning, President Trump posted an AI-generated image to social media. It is based on that photo of Trump from 2024 right after he survived an assassination attempt. He's got blood on his face, and he's hoisting his fist in the air. In the doctored photo, instead of Trump, it's Jensen Huang, and in his hoisted fist, a red bra - a reference, of course, to Nvidia's reinstatement of Huang as CEO. NPR's Andrea Hsu has been speaking with women in tech about that.

ANDREA HSU, BYLINE: When Bo Young Lee learned that Nvidia's board had brought Jensen Huang back, the first word that entered her mind was unfathomable. Then her reaction to President Trump's post...

BO YOUNG LEE: Absolutely flabbergasted.

HSU: For five years, Lee worked as chief diversity officer at Uber. She was brought in in 2018 to turn around the culture following reports of harassment and discrimination. To her, the image seems to be suggesting that Huang is as important as the president. She says that's unbelievable.

LEE: But then, also, the red bra is an indication that, like, it's open hunting season for women.

HSU: The White House has not responded to NPR's request for comment. Ever since the Nvidia scandal broke, Lee has felt that Huang's relationship with Alice Huang and concerns about national security and Nvidia's stock price have overshadowed Huang's behavior in the workplace, specifically his alleged affair with a direct report. She thought there was no way Huang should be allowed to return if he indeed had an affair with an employee.

LEE: Everyone is minimizing that alleged relationship there because of who she is. She's a very senior leader herself, and she makes a lot of money.

HSU: Lee says that shouldn't matter. She argues that people in subordinate roles, even powerful ones, can't properly consent.

LEE: Simply for the fact that there is this power differential.

HSU: Nvidia's board did find that Huang's behavior was, quote, "inconsistent with the company's code of conduct." But this morning in a statement, the board said it voted unanimously to reinstate him, that it was satisfied with respect to Huang's candor and ability to lead Nvidia. Bo Young Lee says the board is sending a message, not just to Nvidia employees but all of Silicon Valley, that it's OK to break the rules as long as you come clean.

LEE: Just be transparent with us.

HSU: Nvidia did not respond to NPR's questions about these concerns. In Silicon Valley, there have been conversations about Huang's alleged workplace transgressions and the power dynamics at play, but people seem reluctant to speak out. NPR reached out to two dozen women who work in tech. Freada Kapor Klein was one of the few willing to talk. She's a social impact investor who's advocated for women and people of color her whole career. She says those conversations are happening, but...

FREADA KAPOR KLEIN: They are much quieter now than they have been in other instances, in other eras.

HSU: Like in 2017 and '18, when a bunch of venture capitalists resigned amid allegations they were sexually harassing female entrepreneurs. To be clear, Huang has not been accused of predatory behavior. Still, to Kapor Klein, his swift comeback is troubling.

KAPOR KLEIN: It is a resounding message that all that matters is money.

HSU: She says if you're thought of as a singular talent...

KAPOR KLEIN: You can violate corporate policy. You can possibly threaten national security. You can make up your own rules as you go as long as you bring in the money.

HSU: Bo Young Lee says Silicon Valley has always had an unhealthy relationship with what she calls its genius founders.

LEE: We elevate these leaders to godlike levels, and that's been done to Mark Zuckerberg, and that's being done to Sam Altman, and that's definitely done to Jensen Huang. You become untouchable at that point.

HSU: What's unfolded at Nvidia has led Kapor Klein to one conclusion.

KAPOR KLEIN: We need guardrails for CEOs, not just for the tools that their companies create.

HSU: She says today's move shows those guardrails don't exist.

Andrea Hsu, NPR News.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

entries.title: Mending relationships over the holidays? Considering a truce? NPR wants to know
entries.summary: Has a political or social issue broken down a relationship that was important to you? Can it be repaired? Tell us what's going on. You might be asked to participate in a possible upcoming segment on All Things Considered.
entries.content:
The divisive American political climate over the last few years has been splintering relationships. Whether you've blocked a high school buddy on social media or cut off a relative, there are some issues that may have felt too big to ignore.

But with the midterms over and holiday season getting started, there might be an incentive to re-start the conversation. If you're considering a truce this season or even a full amends, we want to hear about it.

Fill out the form below, and an NPR producer may reach out to you and your loved one for a conversation.

We will not use your submission in our story until we have communicated with you and obtained your consent to use the details that will be published.

entries.title: 'Medicare for all' is back on the drawing board. Does it stand a better chance this time?
entries.summary: Several newly elected Democratic U.S. senators campaigned on Medicare for All. Could this be the time it actually gets traction?
entries.content:
‘Medicare for all’ is back on the drawing board. Does it stand a better chance this time?

Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.

History doesn't repeat itself, but it does rhyme, as the saying goes. That's certainly true of the coming fight over "Medicare for All."

The midterm elections resulted in victories for several candidates who made universal, government-funded health coverage, or some variation thereof, a central pillar of their campaigns, including new Democratic U.S. senators-elect from Michigan, Maine, Iowa, and Texas. They — and many of their soon-to-be colleagues — say they will push the new Democratic majorities in the House and Senate to finally solve the healthcare affordability problem, which so many voters complained about on the campaign trail.

But while virtually every elected official supports making healthcare available and affordable for all Americans, the details of getting there cleaved the Democratic Party the last several times healthcare topped the national agenda. The Clinton health reform effort in 1993-94 fractured over differences within the Democratic majority, as those who wanted a dramatic overhaul like Medicare for All argued with those who saw incremental changes — such as a public option — as more politically feasible. The Affordable Care Act, which despite incendiary politics made incremental reforms, barely squeaked into law in 2010 after similar disputes..

And, so far, it appears history is about to write another stanza of this epic poem.

"It's cosplay"

So why is something so popular in the abstract so hard to accomplish?

For one thing, most Americans have no real idea what the phrase "Medicare for All" actually means. "It's cosplay," said Nicholas Bagley, a law professor at the University of Michigan who has written about health policy for years. "When you say 'Medicare for All,' people think 'Healthcare — good. We should have more of it.'"

Mollyann Brodie — who oversees KFF's public opinion and survey research program as executive vice president and chief operating officer of the health information nonprofit — points out that in the long history of Medicare for All, support rises and falls dramatically depending on how the policy is described to voters.

"I can move it up to three-quarters [percent approval] if I talk about it being a guaranteed right to healthcare or eliminating insurance premiums and reducing out-of-pocket costs," she said of survey respondents' support, on a recent episode of the What the Health? From KFF Health News podcast. "I can plummet that support down to the 20s if I talk about it requiring people to pay more in taxes or threatening the current Medicare program."

Medicare faces headwinds

A second problem Democrats face is that the Medicare program itself, which covers adults 65 and older and some people with disabilities, is on less-than-firm financial footing. As of this year, the trust fund that underpins the hospital insurance part of the program is projected to become insolvent in 2033.

Costs are rising for Medicare beneficiaries as well. The program requires significant out-of-pocket spending on premiums, deductibles, and coinsurance. At the same time, traditional Medicare fails to cover much-needed services such as dental, vision, hearing, and, most expensively, long-term care. Beefing up Medicare benefits would be expensive and likely require large tax increases, according to most outside estimates.

The new Democratic majorities in Congress will have to decide whether their priority is to reverse the spending cuts made by the Trump administration — both to the Medicaid program for low-income and disabled people and to Affordable Care Act health plans — or to expand coverage and lower costs, turning back time to before President Donald Trump's second term began.

"Expectations are super high among voters right now, and they are demanding action on healthcare costs," Brodie said.

There are already indications that Democratic leaders are listening to the Medicare-for-All wing of their party. A day before being officially nominated as the next speaker of the House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York voiced support for expanding government-funded coverage, including by lowering the age of Medicare eligibility and covering all children.

Of course, even if Democrats can pass legislation to restore what was cut by the GOP, there is every expectation that Trump — who has referred to Medicare for All in the past as "a socialist takeover of our healthcare system" — would veto those efforts. And the new majorities, while large, are not veto-proof.

Finally, Democrats must face a reality that both parties often forget: The larger your majority, the more ideologically diverse it will be. While the next Congress will include more progressives pursuing Medicare for All, it will also have plenty more moderate members from swing districts currently represented by Republicans. It's the reverse of the splits that plagued the GOP in the current Congress, with conservatives from safe red districts pitted against moderates from purplish ones.

A deeper dissatisfaction?

There is one big difference in the coming Democrat-on-Democrat debates compared with those in 1993 and 2009. One thing that has hamstrung Democrats trying to fix the health system is resistance from a plurality, if not a majority, of Americans who are relatively satisfied with their current health coverage. During the Clinton-era health reform debate, those people were represented in the famous "Harry and Louise" ads sponsored by the health insurance industry, featuring a couple at their kitchen table worrying that proposed changes would leave them worse off financially.

KFF's September tracking poll found instead that not only was the professed support for Medicare for All at its highest since the organization started regularly asking about it, but also a majority of respondents said they would support the policy even if it meant eliminating the private insurance industry. That's a first, and a significant change at that. It suggests the public is so fed up with the status quo that they'd rather risk something completely new than stick with what they have.

Of course, that sentiment could change fast when industry opposition revs up its counter-campaign. Still, the survey results suggest the next health reform debate could start with a public ready for something bigger. Now it's up to the people who could make it happen to get on the same page.

HealthBent, a regular feature of KFF Health News, offers insight into and analysis of policies and politics from KFF Health News chief Washington correspondent Julie Rovner, who has covered health care for more than 40 years.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

entries.title: Trump claims credit as Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia
entries.summary: President Trump endorsed the announcement, calling it essential for the success of the company and the economy. He added that the government does not see Huang's return as a national security risk.
entries.content:
Sign up for alerts on breaking news and exclusive reporting from NPR.

Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO of the world's largest chipmaker on Monday, sending the company's stock soaring as President Trump claimed credit for brokering his close ally's return.

It was a stunning reversal of fortune for Huang. He resigned less than two weeks ago, following news reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of being a Chinese spy.

In a statement put out just before the market opened, Nvidia said its board voted unanimously in favor of bringing back Huang after a series of conversations and meetings, as well as input from people at "senior levels" of the U.S. government. "Based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk," the board said.

Nvidia's stock price shot up more than 30% on Monday, helping buoy stock indexes after last week's losses, which were driven by the tech sector.

Trump endorsed the move, calling it the "correct and proper decision" in a social media post. He said Huang's leadership was needed "in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy."

The president had repeatedly urged Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang as CEO in public comments and on social media. In a lengthy interview with CNBC Monday morning, Trump claimed his influence helped Huang get his job back.

"I don't want to say, but basically I was represented at the board," the president said, in response to a question about a report in Semafor that he had called directly into the Nvidia board meeting.

"I spoke to them. Let me just put it that way. And I convinced them," Trump told CNBC. "And I must tell you, it was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week and a half ago."

He later added: "When the stock starts dropping forty, fifty percent, it was a lot easier for me to do it yesterday than it would have been."

Huang stepped down amid a growing scandal

Nvidia, which Huang co-founded and has run for the past 33 years, dominates the market for the chips used to train and run artificial intelligence. Trump and Huang have grown close during the president's second term in office, with Huang becoming one of the most influential business leaders with the president's ear on AI policy. He has successfully lobbied the U.S. government to allow chipmakers to sell some chips to China, although Nvidia's most advanced chips are subject to export controls.

Huang resigned from Nvidia on Nov. 12 after news reports that he had affairs with multiple women, including an Nvidia executive who reported to him. But the most explosive allegation was that he'd engaged in a relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was buying Nvidia chips, whom U.S. officials believed had ties to Chinese intelligence.

The Justice Department has said it is conducting a criminal investigation of Megaspeed for potential chip smuggling.

On Monday, the Commerce Department said it is adding Megaspeed to a list of companies barred from buying advanced technology, including some AI chips, without a U.S. government license.

Megaspeed didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. The company previously denied wrongdoing and said that Alice Huang left the company in 2025 and that it is conducting an internal investigation.

Nvidia's board said as recently as Nov. 17 that it did not intend to reinstate Huang, though Huang publicly said he would return if the board allowed it. On Monday, board chair Harvey Jones said in a statement: "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."

The board said its turnaround followed a series of meetings with Huang that left them satisfied with his "candor and ability to lead" the company. It said its investigation into Huang and the reports he had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort continues and that Huang is "committed to cooperating with it."

In a statement on Monday, Huang said he was "honored" to return. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," he said.

Silicon Valley cheers as questions about Nvidia's governance linger

The board's abrupt reversal was cheered by many Silicon Valley leaders and investors who had joined calls for Huang to return.

"The mistake has been corrected," SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on his social media site X. Gavin Baker, whose firm Atreides Management invests in Nvidia, posted a video of employees applauding Huang as he returned to the chipmaker's headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif. on Monday.

"The idea that this company can only be successful and continue to do what it's doing with that person at the helm ... is the argument made by a lot in Silicon Valley last week and by the president — that Nvidia's success depends on Jensen running it," said Margaret O'Mara, a historian who studies Silicon Valley at the University of Washington.

Some women who have advocated for the tech industry to tackle gender inequality and abuses of power say that for the board to reinstate Huang after previously saying his behavior was "inconsistent" with the company's code of conduct sends a signal to Silicon Valley.

"It is a resounding message that all that matters is money," said Freada Kapor Klein, a social impact investor who's advocated for women and people of color in tech.

Nvidia did not respond to NPR's questions about those concerns.

Huang's reinstatement also raises questions about Nvidia's corporate governance and how the board is weighing short-term considerations against the company's policies, said Rob Lalka, a professor at Tulane University's Freeman School of Business.

"It really was sort of an eye-opening moment to think about how this board, just a few days ago, had said they would not bring Jensen Huang back and that they had voted unanimously for that. There's still an investigation open in their company" into Huang's behavior, Lalka said. "And the board basically went around its entire process that it had set in place for that investigation to put him back into power."

Trump dismisses national security concerns

On Monday, Trump wrote on Truth Social that the government has "no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security," and that Attorney General Todd Blanche says the U.S. "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

Last week Nvidia's board said it had formed a committee to oversee the company's national security policies, compliance with U.S. export controls, and risk management of global trade.

Huang is expected to testify before multiple congressional committees next week.

To explain why it was so important that Huang remain at Nvidia's helm, Trump told CNBC he feared China attempting to bring his expertise to their country.

"I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen, 'Hey, how would you like to come to China?' He's got a little blood in him, you know. He's got a little blood there. 'How would you like to come to China and head up Huawei, okay, and head up one of our companies?'" Trump said. "And you know what? If Jensen was angry enough, if he was treated badly, maybe he could do that."

When CNBC asked Trump if he wasn't worried after he was alerted that Huang was in a relationship with a potential spy, Trump demurred, saying, "I won't get into it."

Following the CNBC interview, Trump celebrated Huang's reinstatement on Truth Social by posting a doctored image invoking a famous photo of the president after the assassination attempt in Butler, Penn., in 2024. In the posted image, Huang is in President Trump's place with blood spattered on his face, raising his fist — holding a red bra — as a flag bearing Nvidia's logo waves in the background.

NPR's Andrea Hsu contributed to this report.

entries.title: Democrats win House by largest margin in 50 years. And, COP31 ends with no deal
entries.summary: Democrats have currently flipped 47 House seats and could flip 49 total. And, climate change talks at COP31 ran two days longer than expected, becoming the longest conference in the summit's history.
entries.content:
AI Impact On Economy, Russia-Ukraine War Spills Into Poland, No Deal At COP31

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Vote counts are concluding for the 2026 midterm elections, revealing a better picture of just how much Democrats dominated. Fifty-six percent of voters chose the Democrats in House races compared to 42% for Republicans. The 14-point gap is the largest margin won by Democrats in 50 years. The party has officially won the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s. Take a look at NPR's breakdown of the U.S. House races, by the numbers.

Artificial intelligence is causing significant swings in the stock market as investors speculate about the future of the technology boom. While AI stocks have driven markets to record highs and bolstered the economy, concerns are growing about a potential bubble. Investors anticipated that AI giant Anthropic's stock market debut last week would lift markets, but instead Wall Street experienced one of its worst weeks in recent times.

  • 🎧 The National Association for Business Economics released a survey asking firms about their AI experiences. NPR's Scott Horsley tells Up First that one in five reported measurable, widespread productivity gains, while about half said they saw some gains, but they weren't widespread. About 30% were either not using AI or felt it was too soon to assess its impact. Austan Goolsbee, head of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, pointed out that the significant investment in AI is already affecting the economy, contributing to inflation by increasing demand for construction materials and electronic components. Although proponents believe AI could eventually help lower costs and limit inflation, Goolsbee tells Horsley that the Federal Reserve must address inflation challenges right now.

Poland has called an emergency NATO session for today after Russia fired three cruise missiles into its territory. The incident highlights the stakes for European countries in Russia's war on Ukraine, prompting nations along NATO's eastern border to seek enhanced air defense support. Poland plans to present proposals to increase surveillance capabilities and deploy more F-35s to intercept incoming missiles and drones.

  • 🎧 Anti-missile systems and NATO flights were activated successfully, but Polish authorities say that poor weather prevented them from intercepting the incoming Russian missiles, according to reporter Teri Schultz. No injuries or damage were reported. More than a year ago, NATO established the Eastern Sentry to enhance air defense after a significant drone swarm from Russia entered Poland. Experts are now scrutinizing potential gaps in this defense. If this attack was deliberate by Moscow, Russia is risking severe consequences by endangering the lives of people on the ground in a NATO country, Schultz says.

Delegates at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, couldn't agree on a plan over the weekend to address fossil fuels, the main cause of climate change. The event ran two days longer than expected, making it the longest in the history of these summits. Nearly 200 nations failed to finalize targets for electrification and financial aid for developing countries, or to address the impacts of climate change. The European Union rejected any conclusion that didn't advocate for a transition away from fossil fuels, while oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia opposed this position. Fossil fuels contribute about 73% of global emissions.

  • 🎧 Ultimately, the EU decided that no COP deal was better than a deal that didn't address fossil fuels, NPR's Rachel Waldholz says. She adds that money was another major issue. Developing nations sought increased support to tackle climate change, noting that they've contributed very little to climate change but often deal with the worst impacts. Wealthy nations agreed to provide funding under the Paris Climate Agreement. The U.S. was absent from the discussions due to the Trump administration's withdrawal from international climate negotiations. Many smaller and developing nations are strong defenders of these talks, viewing them as a vital platform to ensure their voices are heard alongside larger countries, Waldholz says.

Books We Love

NPR's annual reading guide, Books We Love, is back with more than 380 new recommendations from staff and trusted critics. This year's picks span a range of genres, including fiction, cookbooks, children's reads, poetry and science fiction. Don't worry if it looks overwhelming; the interactive filters will help you narrow down your list and find your next great read. And why stop at this year's reads? The Books We Love archive has 14 years of recommendations, so you can discover more than 4,700 amazing books, all in one place. This year's edition of Books We Love is dedicated to Rose Friedman, who edited a dozen editions and worked at NPR for 15 years before her death this year at age 38. Friedman was one of the original founders of Books We Love, formerly known as The Book Concierge. In her honor, start exploring and find something wonderful to read today.

Behind the story

by Maria Godoy, senior science and health editor and correspondent

People had warned me it might be tough to get Amish people to talk to me as a journalist — and probably impossible to get their permission to record their voice. Not a great omen for compelling radio storytelling.

Yet as I headed off to Lancaster County, Pa., last month to report on the biggest and deadliest measles outbreak in the U.S. in decades, I knew I wanted to hear directly from the community hit hardest.

So I turned to some good old shoe-leather reporting. My producer and I mapped out Amish-owned businesses in and around Lancaster County and spent a day driving around from shop to shop. At every stop, we introduced ourselves and explained the focus of our story. We asked Amish people (easily identifiable by their traditional dress) about their views on the measles outbreak and vaccination. While some declined to talk, others opened up about how measles had affected their families and communities, and why they had or hadn't decided to get vaccinated. To my surprise, one woman even let me record her voice.

Outside a farm supply store in a rural town, I met an Amish woman who was visibly pregnant. Measles can have devastating consequences during pregnancy. She told me her husband and two children had gotten vaccinated to protect her and her unborn child. She declined to give me her name at first, then got in a car driven by her hired non-Amish driver. As they exited the parking lot, the driver stopped to ask us what media outlet we were with. "Oh, NPR!" the driver said when we replied. Then she turned to her Amish passenger and told her, "Don't worry, you can trust them."

Part of gaining trust is about showing up, showing respect and really listening. Word gets around that you're trustworthy. Public health officials in Pennsylvania have also been using a similar approach to win the trust of Amish people as they seek to boost vaccination rates in the current outbreak. You can read more about it here.

3 things to know before you go

  1. Bayer could pay up to $7.25 billion to settle lawsuits alleging that its weed-killer Roundup caused cancer. A Missouri judge gave final approval to the nationwide settlement.
  2. South Africa's grassroots program Read Alex is tackling a children's literacy crisis and inspiring kids to write. The initiative culminated in a book launch for an anthology titled From Gomora to the World, showcasing stories written by children.
  3. Orchestra Noir transforms 2000s hip-hop and R&B classics into high-energy, choreographed symphonic shows. Beyond delivering performances, the all-Black ensemble creates a cultural bridge through their post-show ritual, when musicians meet with their multigenerational audiences.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

entries.title: Zelenskyy hails Ukraine's attack on a Russian warship docked at a naval base in Libya
entries.summary: Ukraine carried out an attack on a Russian warship moored at a port in Libya, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, claiming that sea drones sank the navy vessel in a surprise assault.
entries.content:
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine carried out an attack on a Russian warship moored at a port in Libya, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday, claiming that maritime drones sank the navy vessel in a surprise assault the previous day.

Ukrainian forces deployed seven drones in the operation that struck the Russian navy corvette in the Mediterranean, according to Zelenskyy. The ship, the Merkury, was one of Russia's newest vessels, commissioned a year after Moscow launched the 2022 full-scale invasion of its neighbor, he said in a post on X.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov declined to comment on the attack, saying that Russia's Defense Ministry would provide more information "if deemed to be appropriate."

The operation, conducted some 2,400 kilometers (1,500 miles) from the front line in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv's forces.

Ukraine has at times embarrassed Moscow during the war with attacks such as Operation Spiderweb in June 2025, when drones launched from trucks hit over 40 aircraft parked at air bases across Russia. Along the roughly 1,250-kilometer (almost 800-mile) front line snaking through eastern and southern Ukraine, Kyiv's drones and ground robots are helping hold back Russia's bigger army.

At the same time, Russia's missiles and drones have devastated Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter and damaged civilian buildings.

A Russian strike on a five-story apartment block in a village near Kyiv killed 11 people, regional police said Monday. A 7-year-old child and a 79-year-old woman were pulled alive from the rubble after the Sunday morning attack, rescue services said.

Three people were killed Monday in a Russian strike on a hospital in the city of Zaporizhzhia in southern Ukraine, the regional military administration said. Two other people were killed when Russian forces struck a vehicle that bore markings indicating it was evacuating residents from the eastern city of Kramatorsk, authorities said.

Also on Monday, the European Commission proposed a new round of sanctions to keep economic pressure on Moscow, targeting dozens of Russian banks, cracking down on crypto platforms and slapping bans on sports teams and athletes competing under the country's flag.

The proposals, put forward by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, must be endorsed by all 27 European Union member countries before they can enter into force. The process can take weeks, and the planned measures are likely to be modified.

The bloc has already hit more than 4,700 people and entities, including President Vladimir Putin, and several energy companies.

Zelenskyy lauds Ukrainian attacks from Siberia to Libya

Zelenskyy described Sunday's attack as "exemplary" and said "the targets we set were achieved."

"We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons," he said.

Ukraine has hit Russian oil refineries as far away as western Siberia and Russian warships in the Mediterranean, Zelenskyy noted in a video address to a meeting of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.

An oil refinery in Russia's western Rostov region halted work Monday after what Gov. Yuri Slyusar said was a "massive" Ukrainian drone and missile attack that lasted more than six hours. Ukraine's General Staff said the refinery, located just a few dozen kilometers (miles) from the Ukrainian border, can process up to 55 million barrels of oil a year and was on fire after the attack.

Russian officials also reported Monday a Ukrainian attack on industrial sites in Russia's Perm region, more than 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) from Ukraine. One person was killed in the attack, and 56 Ukrainian drones were downed, Perm Gov. Dmitri Makhonin said.

"We keep finding ways to get back on our feet after every Russian attack," Zelenskyy said.

Ukrainian forces also struck the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said Moscow used to transport weapons. He added that the forces also destroyed a Ka-27 military helicopter that was on the Merkury.

Ukrainian forces are operating in western Libya under a covert deal endorsed by the West, using the North African country's territory to strike a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in March, according to Libyan officials.

The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, were operating mainly at an air base in the coastal city of Misrata, but also in other military facilities in the capital of Tripoli and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told The Associated Press earlier this year. They spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential matters.

Sunday's attack severely damaged the Russian corvette at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya, according to two Libyan officials, although Zelenskyy claimed it was sunk.

Benghazi residents heard loud explosions and saw flames at the base early Sunday. Civil defense units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

The vessel had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of an agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, a statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.

The government in eastern Libya sent a letter to U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres and the U.N. Security Council, calling for an international investigation into the potential use of western Libya to prepare and launch the attack.

Libyan officials say 2 sea drones hit Russian warship

Libyan officials who were briefed on the attack told AP that at least four drones were intercepted while two hit the corvette, which is designed to patrol coastal waters and escort other ships.

At least 10 people, including Libyan and Russian nationals, were wounded in the attack, one of the officials said.

The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to talk with reporters.

Ambrey, a U.K.-based maritime security and risk intelligence firm, said that some of the explosions at the Benghazi Naval Base were likely caused by the detonation of ammunition aboard the Merkury.

Hours after the warship attack, another sea drone strike hit a Maltese-flagged commercial vessel sailing off Benghazi, the Libyan coast guard said.

The Russian cargo ship was sanctioned, Ukraine says

Ukraine's Security Service, or SBU, said the cargo ship MV Angara was sanctioned and used to transport Russian military equipment, while the Merkury regularly escorted Russian naval convoys, including guarding the MV Angara.

The drones were delivered to a designated location and launched from a "mother ship" near the target, the SBU said.

Russian defenses tried to intercept the attacking drones, it said.

"Ukraine's defense forces have once again shown that the Russian navy and its logistics have no safe routes," the SBU said.

entries.title: Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?
entries.summary: Wellness influencers say mushroom supplements can help with your gut health, focus and immune system. Here is where research suggests there are some links.
entries.content:
Growing up in the French Alps, Julie Daoust fell for mushrooms early in life.

"So as a kid, we'd go out and forage," she recalls. "We'd come across species like lion's mane or reishi. And I became more and more interested in those species."

Daoust went on to get a Ph.D. in chemistry, searching nature for novel pharmaceuticals. Her work ultimately led her back to mushrooms, a group of organisms to which humans are more closely related than plants. And yet, many of our modern medicines and therapeutics come from plants.

"Mushrooms share a lot more in terms of their biochemistry with us than plants do," says Daoust, which means "you have more chances of finding something that's going to have bioactivity in a human than you would with other source organisms."

Daoust is now vice president of science and innovation at Monterey Nutra, a company that specializes in the genetics and cultivation of mushrooms and sells fungal extracts and powders. Her team focuses not on the poisonous varieties, nor the psychedelic ones that contain psilocybin. Rather, they are interested in the functional or medicinal mushrooms that Daoust likens to tiny cauldrons of potentially useful molecules.

"We love to look for soft things that can't run away very fast," says Daoust, "because they typically produce really interesting chemistry to defend themselves or to communicate with others in their environment to survive."

The claim

Daoust says that certain types of fungi may have specific uses.

For instance, lion's mane — a soft chandelier of a fungus — may aid cognition. Reishi and turkey tail, which are mushrooms that grow as hard brown scales on decomposing trees, could bolster immune health.

And on social media, influencers and advertisers promise that medicinal mushrooms, taken as supplements, can slow aging and improve energy levels, focus and immune health.

The evidence

Robust clinical trials proving such connections — and their safety — are largely lacking, according to Abby Langer, a registered dietitian based in Toronto. "In my opinion, I don't think that there's much evidence for functional mushrooms as of now," she says.

Langer says mushrooms accumulate and concentrate the materials in the ground they're grown in, both good and bad — so one has to be cautious.

Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

She grants that in certain communities (in parts of Asia, for instance), mushrooms have been incorporated into their healing practices for generations. However, "just because something has been used for a long time doesn't mean that it's safe, that it's effective, that the dosing has been established," Langer says. "There are a lot of unknowns."

Still, she acknowledges that empirical support for the potential positive impacts of mushrooms is growing. "The clinical research on specific functional mushroom products is young," she says, "but it's accumulating fast and already includes some impressive results."

Mushrooms are a good source of vitamin D2 and antioxidants. Their cell walls contain beta-glucan, which has been linked to gut health, including a lower risk of Crohn's Disease, and immune response. Research into the effects of mushrooms on cognition have been mixed.

In addition, there's work out of Japan looking at how PSK, a purified extract from turkey tail, improved immune response in cancer patients. A meta-analysis considered 8,009 patients in eight randomized controlled trials who had undergone surgical removal of a gastric tumor and in almost all cases chemotherapy. Those who were also given PSK showed a 12% reduction in risk of death.

"This is not something that we brush off," says Santhosshi Narayanan, an integrative oncologist based at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center who recognizes the potential of PSK.

Even so, she admits that this "does not mean that PSK or any mushrooms alone cures cancer. It just shows to us that we need to pay attention to these natural products." Narayanan says there's still a lot to figure out with this particular extract, especially for populations outside Japan with different genetics or treatment regimes who might experience unwanted side effects.

"We need to do more research and understand how we can use it," she says. "Like which people, which type of patients benefit from which type of mushroom — because that itself is a whole science."

Narayanan and her colleagues also surveyed 2,349 studies examining the relationship between medicinal mushrooms and cancer, but only 39 were robust enough to be included in their 2023 analysis. Of that subset, "31 studies showed beneficial effects of the mushrooms, resulting in improved quality of life, reduced [side effect] profiles of different chemotherapeutic drugs, improved anti-inflammatory and anti-metastatic effects, and improved [disease-free survival] as well as [overall survival] in a few trials," according to the report.

Six studies didn't reveal any advantage and two highlighted worse outcomes. Overall, the analysis was unable to make clear conclusions about "the complex biological effects of mushrooms on the immune system in cancer."

The bottom line

In Narayanan's estimation, there's not yet enough evidence to support routine clinical use in cancer treatment.

And Langer recommends considering a few nutrition basics before introducing a supplement for gut health or cognition. "Take a closer look at what you're eating, how you're eating, when you're eating," she advises, "and see if there's any tweaks that you need to make."

Maybe it's possible to eat more fiber or protein, reduce consumption of alcohol or sugar-sweetened beverages, skip fewer meals, or eat out less often, she says.

"There's so many things that people can potentially improve on," Langer says, "before adding something else that's promised to be this panacea for everything that ails you."

entries.title: K is for kindness, but families worry the world has less of it
entries.summary: A decade after first asking families about kindness, Sesame Workshop asked parents similar questions. They responded that their kids are getting kinder even as the wider world becomes less so.
entries.content:
Parents and caregivers of young children worry the world has become less kind, and they now value empathy in their children over good manners, compassion over confidence.

Those are just a few highlights from a new survey of families' views on kindness from Sesame Workshop, the education nonprofit behind Sesame Street.

"Caregivers see the world as much more unkind to their young children than they did in 2016," says Kim Foulds, vice president of research and evaluation at Sesame Workshop, "but the reason to hope is that parents see their children as more kind, more empathetic, more resilient than they did in 2016."

The new "K is for Kind Study 2026" comes 10 years after the original "K is for Kind: A National Survey on Kindness and Kids," and it offers a remarkable glimpse at how families' feelings about kindness have shifted, in some cases dramatically, over a decade defined by the rise of social media and bitter political polarization.

Monday's release also coincides with the debut of Sesame Street's 57th season, which will focus on kindness and compassion in action.

Let's start with that bad news: Compared to survey results from 2016, caregivers today have a much darker view of the world:

  • About 80% often worry the world is an unkind place for children. That's a nearly 11-percentage-point increase since 2016;
  • Fifty-four percent say kindness is not a priority for most people, a 10-point increase since 2016; and
  • On a scale of 1 to 5, caregivers give the average American a 2.8 for kindness.

Taken together, the data shows a worrying shift in the way families perceive the world — as a place with more rough edges that is less attuned to the needs of their young children. To draw these conclusions, Sesame Workshop conducted 2,080 interviews in October with a nationally representative sample of caregivers of children ages 3-8 years old across all 50 states.

The good news, Foulds says, is that, while caregivers "are concerned about the division and unkindness they see in the wider world, their experience of their own children is much more immediate and hopeful."

Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

This manifests in a few key ways. First, in parents' own values for their children:

  • Caregivers say they value their child being considerate (68%) over being smart (32%);
  • They value compassion (56%) over confidence (44%), a big swing of 8 percentage points compared to when the same question was asked in the 2016 survey; and
  • They value empathy (64%) over manners (36%) — an even bigger swing of 24 points compared to a decade ago.

In short, parents and caregivers say their values are shifting toward kindness. That shift, in turn, is showing up in the behaviors families say they're seeing from their kids.

  • A whopping 92% of caregivers rate their child highly for kindness, a 5-percentage point increase since 2016;
  • Some 74% of caregivers rate their child highly for resilience, a 12-point increase;
  • And 56% gave their child a low anxiety rating, an 8-point improvement over 2016.

And that leads to what Foulds says was one of the most startling — and hopeful — results from the survey: 94% of caregivers said, when their child does something kind, they do it on their own, without encouragement or nudging.

"The child was seeing the opportunity to be kind themselves," Foulds says. "And I thought that was an incredibly beautiful, incredibly powerful finding to see how kindness is showing up in action in young children's lives."

These encouraging numbers come with one grain of salt: It's not unusual for caregivers to have a rosier view of their own children or their own local circumstances than of the wider world. In fact, this is a common phenomenon in education research, for example, where families often give America's schools low marks but high marks to their child's school and their child's teacher.

While this phenomenon likely influenced today's results, too, Sesame's twin surveys still offer a remarkable view of how caregivers' own views have shifted over the past decade.

What is kindness? The survey offers answers there, too. Caregivers talk about their children sharing in a way that requires them to give something up, connecting across languages and culture, making room for different abilities and including children who have been left out.

The survey also includes caregiver testimonials.

The parent of a 4-year-old told researchers, "He has a child in his class that is neurodivergent, which is different than him, and he is always helpful, always kind, always says 'Hi' whenever he sees this child for class and tries to be a good friend."

The parent of a 6-year-old told researchers, "My child was friends with an autistic child who is nonverbal. My child figured out a way to communicate with him, even though he could not express himself with words."

In the new survey, 85% of caregivers say it's "extremely important" to promote kindness, which is what Sesame Street's latest season will do when it debuts today on both Netflix and PBS KIDS.

"Each story really focuses on kindness, compassion, big feelings, and it's really designed to inspire children to carry the lessons beyond the screen," Foulds says. "We want the viewing to be the beginning of something, not the beginning and end."

In one scene from the new season, Muppets Elmo and Abby realize their choices have made a playmate feel left out and alone. They feel badly and decide to comfort and include him.

As one of the show's grown-ups reminds them, "One little help is all it takes."

Edited by Nirvi Shah and Nicole Cohen
